title: Incident & On-Call
description: Severity, mitigation, bridge updates, and calm urgency.

items.scenario: You are primary on-call. PagerDuty fires for elevated 5xx on the checkout API. Error rate is 18% and rising. You have joined the incident bridge.
items.prompt: What is the clearest first update to the bridge?

choices.text: Something is broken in checkout. Looking into it.
We are seeing elevated 5xx on checkout API, currently about 18% and rising. I am investigating root cause and will share a mitigation plan in five minutes.
This might be related to yesterday's deploy, but I am not sure yet.
Can someone else take a look? I just got paged.

items.explanation: Good bridge updates state impact, metric, ownership, and next checkpoint. Vague language or speculation without a plan slows response.

items.scenario: You confirmed a bad config rollout caused the outage. Rollback is ready and will take about three minutes.
items.prompt: How do you announce the mitigation on the bridge?

choices.text: Rolling back the bad config now. ETA three minutes. I will confirm once error rate returns to baseline.
I found the issue. Trust me, this should fix it.
We need approval from leadership before rolling back.
Everyone stand by while I try a few things.

items.explanation: State the action, ETA, and how you will verify success. That keeps the bridge aligned and calm.

items.scenario: Customer success asks for a public status update while you are still mitigating. Leadership wants customer-safe language.
items.prompt: Which customer-facing update is most appropriate right now?

choices.text: Our checkout service is currently degraded. We have identified the cause and are applying a fix. We will update again within 15 minutes.
A junior engineer pushed a broken config and broke payments.
Everything is fine; please ignore any errors you see.
We do not know what is happening and cannot estimate recovery.

items.explanation: External updates should be factual, non-blaming, and include a next update window without leaking internal finger-pointing.

items.scenario: Your shift ends in 20 minutes. An SEV-2 is still open but stable after mitigation. Secondary is online.
items.prompt: What is the best handoff message?

choices.text: I am signing off. Good luck.

SEV-2 checkout 5xx is mitigated via config rollback. Error rate is back to baseline. Remaining work: confirm dashboards for 30 minutes and draft the incident timeline. Docs and Slack thread linked in the ticket.
It is mostly fine now, just watch it.
I fixed everything, so you can close the incident.

items.explanation: A strong handoff includes current state, mitigation already applied, remaining risks/tasks, and pointers to context.

items.scenario: Two engineers start debugging different hypotheses at once and talk over each other on the bridge.
items.prompt: As incident commander, what should you say?

choices.text: Everyone stop talking. I will decide alone.
Let's parallelize clearly: Alex owns DB connection pool checks, Mira owns recent deploy diffs. Please post findings in the thread; I will synthesize next steps in three minutes.
Just keep trying whatever you think is right.
We should wait until tomorrow to debug properly.

items.explanation: Incident command reduces chaos by assigning owners, channels, and a sync cadence.

items.scenario: A vendor API is timing out. Your service depends on it. A full outage is unlikely, but checkout latency is high for 12% of users.
items.prompt: How do you frame severity to leadership?

choices.text: This is a total outage; we should wake everyone.
Treating this as SEV-2: partial degradation affecting about 12% of checkout users due to vendor timeouts. We enabled stricter timeouts and a fallback path; monitoring recovery.
Not our problem — the vendor is broken.
Users always complain; no need to escalate.

items.explanation: Severity framing needs impact scope, cause hypothesis, and what you already did — not blame or understatement.

items.scenario: You need a database failover. It may cause a brief write interruption. Product asks if they can announce a maintenance window now.

choices.text: Do not announce anything; just fail over silently.
Yes — please announce a short maintenance for write operations. Planned failover starts in 10 minutes and should complete within five minutes. I will confirm when writes are healthy.
Tell customers the database is unstable and may corrupt data.
Ask customers to stop using the product indefinitely.

items.explanation: Coordinate a clear, time-bound customer message with operational reality and a confirmation step.

items.scenario: A teammate suggests restarting all pods immediately without checking recent changes.

choices.text: That idea is useless.
Before a full restart, let's check the last deploy and error signatures for two minutes. If it still looks like a bad process state, we can restart a canary first.
Sure, restart everything right now.
I refuse to do anything you suggest.

items.explanation: Push back with a safer sequence and rationale, not with personal criticism.

items.scenario: The incident is resolved. Leadership asks in Slack whether engineering 'messed up again.'
items.prompt: What is the best immediate reply?

choices.text: Yes, the team failed again.
Service is restored. We will share a blameless timeline and concrete follow-ups in the postmortem within 24 hours, including detection and prevention gaps.
Please do not ask that in public Slack.
It was entirely the vendor's fault, so no postmortem is needed.

items.explanation: Redirect from blame to restoration status and a structured learning process.

items.scenario: You are writing a short Slack update for stakeholders who are not on the bridge.

choices.text: Still looking.
Impact: checkout errors elevated. Status: mitigated via config rollback at 14:12 UTC. Current: error rate normal. Next: monitor for 30 minutes and open postmortem doc.
Lots of moving parts; hard to explain.
Please join the bridge if you care.

items.explanation: Stakeholder updates work best as Impact → Status → Current → Next.
